Two probes show walker disagreement despite identical underlying text, which I traced to walker behavior rather than document divergence: for W6, walker B surfaced a real corollary (a fill-value change on a layer with no edge/padding tiles is byte-invisible to every register check) that is equally true of edition A's identical text, so it is not a loss B introduced; for W11, walker B flagged a tension between Section 7.2's Note and Section 20.4's explicit carve-out that I read, on close inspection of the identical text in both editions, as resolved by Section 20.4's own decisive sentence (so for an implemented type only the PE bit bites) -- walker B's Note-based objection is itself scoped to the not-implemented case in its own final sentence, so I register this as a probable REPORTER_ERROR by walker B rather than a specification ambiguity, and in any case it is not an A-vs-B fidelity issue since the text is identical. W8 showed a similar depth asymmetry: walker B used a closed-core foreclosure argument (Section 12.1/R-TYP-01, Section 2.3) that is equally available from edition A's identical text but that walker A did not invoke. Separately, walker B's own disclosure states it did not read Sections 22-24 or the appendices of edition B; my full-corpus diff confirms those sections are textually unchanged between editions, so this reading-depth asymmetry did not cause either walk to miss an edition-specific difference. No LOSS, ADDITION, or CONTRADICTION between the two editions survived scrutiny anywhere in the writer-charter's scope or in the full-corpus sweep beyond it.</summary>

findings.title: W11: walker B's ambiguity verdict misreads a sentence that decides the case, identically in both editions
findings.detail: Both editions state, immediately before Section 20.4's preservation table and identically in each, that the MU=1 row reaches only a type the updater does not implement, so for an implemented type only the PE bit bites. This directly decides W11's scenario: an updater implementing an unregistered type whose external definition fixes MU=1/PE=0. Since the type is implemented, the MU=1 no-drop row does not reach it, only PE=0 governs, and a drop is licensed. Walker B treats this as in tension with Section 7.2's Note, which says MU=1's PE bit is read as 1 whatever is stored, calling the question underdetermined. But that Note's own final sentence is itself scoped to the not-implemented case (an updater that does not implement an MU=1 record's type never drops the record), so it does not state an unconditional rule covering W11's implemented-but-unregistered case; Section 20.4's explicit carve-out, two sentences before the table, is the one sentence that speaks directly to that case. Since the cited text is byte-identical in A and B, this is not an edition fidelity issue -- it is walker B treating as live a tension that walker A, correctly on this reading, treated as resolved.
findings.quotation_a: Its MU = 1 row reaches only a type the updater does not implement -- an updater implements both registered types and understands an unregistered type it implements from its definition, modifying their records as Section 20.3 and that definition provide -- so for an implemented type only the PE bit bites
findings.quotation_b: Its MU = 1 row reaches only a type the updater does not implement -- an updater implements both registered types and understands an unregistered type it implements from its definition, modifying their records as Section 20.3 and that definition provide -- so for an implemented type only the PE bit bites
findings.byte_level_rationale: Both editions carry the identical decisive sentence and the identical Note, so an implementation built from A alone and one built from B alone would reach the same answer either way; this finding is about a walker's reading of a shared text, not about any edition-sourced byte or verdict difference.

findings.title: W6: the padding-silent fill-change gap walker B flags is present identically in edition A, not B-specific
findings.detail: Walker B's finding writerb-01 observes that a commit barred from changing a stored-tile layer's channel fill (Section 20.3 step 4) is nonetheless byte-invisible to every conformance check wherever the layer has no edge or padding tiles for that channel, since T4/R-SER-05, the only register row that checks padding-position content against the declared fill, has nothing to check and no other row fires either. I confirmed via direct grep and side-by-side read that Section 11.3's padding-position definition, Section 20.3 step 4's fixed-declarations bar, and the Section 21.4 T4 row are byte-identical in edition A. The same gap therefore exists in edition A's text as surely as in B's; walker A's own W6 answer did not pursue this corollary, but nothing in A's text closes it.
findings.quotation_a: A padding position does not encode, for each channel it carries, that channel's recorded fill value | interleaved numeric fill bytes; interleaved bool fill byte; planar numeric plane fill bytes; packed planar bool plane fill bit | verifier | certification | R-SER-05
findings.quotation_b: A padding position does not encode, for each channel it carries, that channel's recorded fill value | interleaved numeric fill bytes; interleaved bool fill byte; planar numeric plane fill bytes; packed planar bool plane fill bit | verifier | certification | R-SER-05
findings.byte_level_rationale: The T4 register row and its governing Section 11.3/20.3 text are byte-identical between editions, confirmed by grep, so an implementation built from A alone and one built from B alone face the identical detection gap; the divergence this finding describes is between two conforming writers under either single edition, not between the two editions.

findings.title: W8: walker B's closed-core foreclosure argument rests on text equally present and unused in edition A
findings.detail: Walker B argues W8's literal premise, a conforming rewriter carrying forward a layer whose sample type it does not implement, cannot occur, because Section 12.1's closed, fully-core 13-type list with R-CNF-03/R-CNF-06 means a tool missing one is not a conforming reader or updater at all, and then answers the nearest on-document analogue anyway. Walker A answers only the nearest-analogue question, without raising the foreclosure point. I confirmed Section 12.1's exactly-thirteen-sample-types rule and Section 2.3's reader/updater conformance clauses are word-for-word identical in both editions, so the foreclosure argument was equally available to walker A from edition A's own text. This is a depth-of-engagement difference between the two walks, not a text difference between the editions.
